title: Chapter 27: Maybe Tomorrow
content: Frost on the cable, and the cable is new, and the frost makes it look like something that has been there a hundred years.

Wren is at the landing at ten past six with a torch in her teeth and a grease gun in her hand, and the winch takes eleven pumps and the sheave takes four, and the pin takes a quarter turn with the spanner and no more.
Pin, apron, bell. She does them in his order because his order is the only one she has.

The cable was strung on Thursday by two men from the county road department who had never done it before and who took nine hours and asked her four times if the sag looked right. It is forty feet of steel with a new thimble, and it holds the ramp square when the water comes up, and it has been greased twice since Friday.
The old cable is coiled by the shed, cut at one end, and she has not decided what to do with it and does not intend to decide today.
The light comes at twenty past six, grey and low, and the river comes with it, brown and steady at four feet, and the far bank comes up out of the dark like a thing remembered.

There is a bronze plaque on the pilaster by the ramp. It went on with four screws on Thursday afternoon, and it says SABLE RIVER CABLE FERRY, MILE 9, BUILT 1908, LISTED ON THE STATE REGISTER OF HISTORIC PLACES, 20 NOVEMBER 2026.

The woman from the state preservation office stood in the cold for an hour and looked at the hull and wrote in her report that the names are an accretion of interpretive value and are to be preserved.
Wren has read that sentence eleven times. It is the finest thing anybody has ever said about the ferry.
At twenty to seven the siren goes.

It is the new horn, on the new pole at the gate house, and the operator on duty runs it for thirty seconds because the state's order says it must be tested every day for the first thirty days. The sound is lower than the old one. It comes down the valley and goes out over the water and comes back off the far bank.

Everybody on the landing stops. Ruthie stops with a tray of cups in her hands. Bram stops with his foot on the ramp. Otis Pell, who is eighty-four and has been standing at the rail since half past six, turns his head and listens to the whole thirty seconds with his eyes shut.
The water does not move.
"That is what it sounds like," Otis says, "when nothing happens."
Nobody answers him. The siren stops and the river goes on going by and the cups get handed out.
Mars comes down the bank at a quarter to seven with a printout in her fist and her lanyard outside her coat, because she is on duty now and wants everybody to know it.
"Forty-one files," she says. "The Division has set a calendar. Three on the second of December, eleven in January, the rest in batches through April. They have to answer each one in writing."
"Who is they."

"The county. The Authority is not the respondent on the files." Mars hands her the sheet. "That is the thing nobody has understood. They were never the Authority's files. They were always the county's, and the county has been waiting for a doctor who died in 2009."
Wren reads the three names at the top of the December column. Pike. Deeds. Nunn.
"Pike is first."
"He is first."
She folds the sheet and puts it in her coat and does not say anything yet, because a name on a calendar is not a certificate, and she has learned that difference the hard way and at some cost.
Celia Reeve comes down the lane at a quarter to seven with a bag over her shoulder and her town shoes in her hand and boots on her feet.
"I am crossing," she says. "The eleven forty from Columbus. I have to be on the west bank by eight."
"You are early."
"I am always early. It is the only thing my mother gave me that I can use."
She puts the bag down and takes something out of her coat pocket and holds it out. It is the brass key with the paper tag.
"It opens nothing now. She had the lock changed on Tuesday." Celia's mouth does what it does. "Keep it anyway. It is the only thing in that house that was ever any use to anybody."
Wren puts it in her pocket with the paint receipt and the badge.
"April?" she says.

"There is not going to be an April." Celia looks at the hull, at the names, at the ones she can read from here. "He is in Columbus. Not the Center of Engineering. He sizes culverts for a company in Gahanna and he calls me on Sundays and does not say anything for a while and then says he has to go."
"All right."

"It is not all right. It is just true." She picks up her bag. "I filed the exhibit. I am not going to be the woman who filed the exhibit for the rest of my life. I am going to be the woman who sells hospital equipment in Dayton and visits her mother at Christmas, and if that is a small life, it is mine."
At seven the county's man comes with the lease in a plastic sleeve and the insurance policy behind it, and Wren signs both on the counter in the shed with a pen that is chained to the counter.
The lease is one dollar a year. The insurance is the policy that lapsed in June, reinstated, with the county named as loss payee, and Elias's name taken off it and hers written in.
She hangs the policy on the wall next to the tariff, where people can see it, because a piece of paper on a wall is the only proof this town has ever believed.

Beside it, in a frame from the hardware store, is the certificate. The word in the box is MISADVENTURE and the findings under it run to three sentences and name the gate and the hour, and she has stopped needing the box to say anything else.
Then she takes the new log out of the tin.
It is blue, the same size as the old one, so that it fits in the tin, and Mars brought it from a stationery shop in Columbus in October and has been carrying it around in her bag ever since.

The old log is on the shelf with four thousand names in it and a water stain through the middle, and the last page ends on the twelfth of September with nine names and a fare column that says PAID nine times, in his hand.
Wren opens the new book at page one and sets it on the counter.
Then she takes the stamp out of the tin.

It is brass on a wooden handle worn smooth at the top, and the die reads AUBREY'S FERRY, MILE 9, SABLE RIVER, and he used it on the backs of the IOUs so that a man who could not pay still went home with a receipt in his pocket.
Hollis Drane is standing by the counter with his coat buttoned right for once. He puts an ink pad down without being asked.
"It is county property," he says. "I am tired of county property."
She inks the die and presses it on page one, square, and the words come up clean and black and a little low.
Then she writes the date herself. 21 November 2026.
Then, under it, in the first line of the book, she writes her own name.
In the fare column she writes FERRYMAN, which is not a fare, and which is the first thing in four thousand pages that her grandfather would have argued with.
He said girl when he was pleased and Wren when he was not, and she has not heard either since September, and she hears the first one now, standing at a counter with a brass stamp in her hand.
Bram comes up the ramp with the ticket tin and stops when he sees the page.
"You are in the book."
"I am in the book."
"He never put himself in the book."

"He never had to." She turns the book around so it faces him. "Write the fares. Write them the way he did. Name, date, and if they pay, PAID, and if they do not, IOU, and do not put a line through anything, because a line through a name is the one thing he would not have."
Bram takes the pen.
Otis Pell crosses first, with his two sticks and a photograph in his coat pocket, going to the county to ask about his father, who is not on any calendar at all.

Ruthie crosses with a box of sandwiches for the west bank crew. Mars crosses because she has never crossed on the new cable. Junie Hale crosses with a shopping list. Hollis Drane crosses for the first time since 2007 and says so at the ramp, to nobody, and then steps aboard like a man getting into a cold bath.
Celia crosses with her bag and stands at the bow and does not look back at the east bank, which is the only way to leave a place.
A woman with two children crosses to get to the school bus on the west road, because the east road is still under water at the second culvert.
Nine passengers and a deckhand and a ferryman.
At ten past seven Wren puts her hand on the winch lever and the cable lifts out of the water and drips and the ramp comes up and the ferry moves off the east bank for the first time since September.
It takes four minutes and eleven seconds.
Nobody says anything for the first minute. Then Otis Pell says, to the water, "Well," and that is the whole of the ceremony.
On the west bank they get off and Bram takes the fares and writes them in the book in his flat Cleveland hand, and the names go down under hers, and the page starts to look like a page.
She comes back empty, which the rules allow, and the sun is up over the ridge and the frost is going off the cable in steam.
There is a line on the east bank.

It goes down the ramp and along the bank and around the boat shed and past the sign that says NINE PASSENGERS, and there are people in it with coffees and people in it with children and one man in it with a folding chair, and Ruthie has set up a table at the top with a box of cups and is charging a dollar and putting the dollars in the coffee can.
Wren ties off and sets the ramp and looks at the line, and the line looks back at her, and nobody waves, because it is not that kind of town.
A woman near the front has a child's hand in hers and a folder under her arm, and she has been in the Annex queue enough times that Wren knows her face and not her name.
She steps up to the ramp and says, "When will the rest of them be certified?"
Wren puts her hand on the wheel and looks at the water, which is going where it always goes and does not care what anybody writes about it.
"Maybe tomorrow," she says.
She means it the way other people mean today.
highlight: Frost on the new cable, a full boat at dawn, and Wren saying maybe tomorrow the way other people say today.
